abstract: Industrial automated reasoning demands the rapid, repeated extraction of insights from complex formulas. Knowledge compilation into the Deterministic Decomposable Negation Normal Form (d-DNNF) addresses this by reducing natively intractable tasks to polynomial-time operations. We present decdnnf_rs, a performant framework for executing advanced reasoning queries directly on d-DNNF circuits. The library provides unified support for Satisfiability, Model Counting, Disjoint Model Enumeration, Direct Access, and Uniform Sampling. Crucially, decdnnf_rs handles dynamic contexts through implicit conditioning via weight propagation, avoiding the computational overhead of explicit graph modification. It also incorporates dynamic smoothness tracking to maintain a compact memory footprint. Bridging theoretical advancements with robust software engineering, decdnnf_rs offers an optimized toolset for exact and stochastic reasoning.

      Abstract
Industrial automated reasoning demands the rapid, repeated extraction of insights from complex
formulas. Knowledge compilation into the Deterministic Decomposable Negation Normal Form
(d-DNNF) addresses this by reducing natively intractable tasks to polynomial-time operations. We
present decdnnf_rs, a performant framework for executing advanced reasoning queries directly on
d-DNNF circuits. The library provides unified support for Satisfiability, Model Counting, Disjoint
Model Enumeration, Direct Access, and Uniform Sampling. Crucially, decdnnf_rs handles dynamic
contexts through implicit conditioning via weight propagation, avoiding the computational overhead
of explicit graph modification. It also incorporates dynamic smoothness tracking to maintain a
compact memory footprint. Bridging theoretical advancements with robust software engineering,
decdnnf_rs offers an optimized toolset for exact and stochastic reasoning.

 1      Introduction

Propositional logic provides the formal foundation for knowledge representation and reasoning
in many areas of Artificial Intelligence [7]. Its utility is evident in diverse subfields such as
Explainable AI (XAI) [18], automated reasoning [4], and decision support [33]. However,
the practical application of propositional logic is constrained by the inherent complexity of
its core inference tasks: satisfiability (SAT) is NP-complete [12], while counting problems
such as #SAT are #P-complete. These complexity barriers often prevent the use of standard
solvers in environments requiring real-time or low-latency responses.
    Industrial requirements further emphasize this problem, as systems must often scale
to massive problem instances under high query volumes. A notable example is AWS’s
Zelkova engine [34], which handles billions of daily verification queries. Similarly, in the
automotive industry, manufacturers such as Mercedes-Benz [37] and Toyota [17] must manage
configuration spaces involving trillions of potential vehicle variants. The challenge is even
more pronounced in probabilistic reasoning for medical diagnosis or risk assessment using
Bayesian and Markov networks [15]. In these domains, answering a single query often requires
solving a #P-hard problem, which is computationally prohibitive for interactive use.

           Knowledge Compilation (KC) offers a principled approach to overcoming these bottle-
       necks [10, 19]. By shifting the computational effort to an offline phase, KC transforms
       propositional formulas into target representations that support polynomial-time queries. The
       Deterministic Decomposable Negation Normal Form (d-DNNF) is one such representation,
       particularly valued for making Weighted Model Counting (WMC) tractable. The primary
       utility of d-DNNF in industrial contexts, from product configuration [1, 32] to system verific-
       ation [2], is its ability to support repeated, efficient reasoning. Practitioners in these fields
       require rapid execution of fundamental queries, including Satisfiability, Model Enumeration,
       Model Counting, Direct Access, and Uniform Sampling. While these tasks are intractable
       on raw CNF formulas, they become efficient operations once the formula is compiled into a
       d-DNNF.
           In this paper, we present decdnnf_rs, a high-performance framework designed to bridge
       the gap between d-DNNF theory and practical application. decdnnf_rs is implemented in
       Rust to ensure memory safety and high execution speed, and is structured as a modular
       system consisting of a core library and a companion command-line interface (CLI). While
       the CLI provides a convenient entry point for standard queries, the library is designed for
       direct integration into performance-critical applications. To facilitate its use across different
       ecosystems, we provide both C and Python bindings, allowing developers to leverage our
       optimized reasoning engine within broader software pipelines. decdnnf_rs shares similarities
       with the existing ddnnife [38] tool but introduces a key advantage: dynamic smoothness
       tracking. This feature enables the execution of requests requiring this property without
       increasing circuit size. More significantly, it opens the door for specialized algorithms like
       partial model enumeration [26].
           The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the core
       concepts of knowledge compilation and the d-DNNF language. Section 3 details the reasoning
       queries supported by decdnnf_rs and discusses their underlying algorithmic implementations.
       Section 4 provides a comprehensive overview of the tool itself, covering its modular system
       architecture, command-line interface (CLI) capabilities, and the integration of its C and
       Python bindings. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines promising directions
       for future work.

2.1    d-DNNF Representation
The Deterministic Decomposable Negation Normal Form (d-DNNF) is a Boolean circuit
fragment represented as a rooted Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) ⟨V, E⟩. The leaves of the
DAG are labeled with literals or the constants ⊤, ⊥. Internal nodes are either decomposable
                                                             V
∧ gates or deterministic ∨ gates. An AND gate N = Ni satisfies decomposability if the
                                                                                               W
variables in the sub-circuits of its children are pairwise disjoint. An OR gate N = Ni
satisfies determinism if its children are pairwise logically inconsistent. The size |Σ| corresponds
to the total number of edges in the DAG. As a language, d-DNNF is universal and can
represent any propositional theory [13].
    Most modern compilers (such as C2D [14], Dsharp [31], d4 [29], and SharpSAT-TD [21])
produce a specialized form known as decision-DNNF. In this variant, deterministic OR gates
are structured as decision nodes ite(x, N1 , N2 ), where the decision variable x is absent from
the sub-circuits N1 and N2 . These decomposable decision graphs [20] can be converted to
d-DNNF in linear time by replacing each ite node with the fragment (¬x ∧ N1 ) ∨ (x ∧ N2 ).

▶ Example 2 (Ex. 1 cont.). An equivalent d-DNNF representation for Ψ is given by Φ =
((¬a ∧ b) ∨ (a ∧ ¬b)) ∧ (c ∨ (¬c ∧ d)). The d-DNNF corresponding to Φ is depicted in Figure 1.

   The d-DNNF language is a highly expressive general framework that strictly encompasses
several well-known tractable subclasses, such as Sentential Decision Diagrams (SDD) [16]
and Ordered Binary Decision Diagrams (OBDD) [9]. Because these languages maintain
the core structural properties of decomposability and determinism, decdnnf_rs is fully
capable of executing queries on them, provided the circuits are serialized into a compatible
representation.

           To ensure broad compatibility, decdnnf_rs parses a standard, plain-text circuit format
       originally popularized by the d4 compiler (and maintained in its recent iteration, d4v2). This
       format specifies the d-DNNF as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) using a simple, line-by-line
       topological description, and is fully documented at https://github.com/jm62300/d4/tree/
       main/demo/compiler. By standardizing on this syntax, decdnnf_rs can seamlessly ingest
       and process compiled artifacts not only from d4, but also from other modern knowledge
       compilers that adhere to this structural format, including translated SDDs and OBDDs.
           Ultimately, the practical appeal of the d-DNNF language stems from its computational
       efficiency for automated reasoning, rendering several typically hard queries tractable. Spe-
       cifically, fundamental operations such as checking satisfiability, applying conditioning, and
       performing model counting [13] operate in linear time relative to the circuit size. Further-
       more, the representation supports advanced algorithms for direct access [11, 8], uniform
       sampling [36], and model enumeration with polynomial delay [19].


        3     Queries Handled by decdnnf_rs
       The practical appeal of d-DNNF lies in its ability to solve complex reasoning tasks effi-
       ciently [26, 27, 5]. In industrial contexts, such as product configuration or probabilistic
       inference, practitioners require the rapid extraction of insights from dynamic data. Con-
       sequently, it is often necessary to query the d-DNNF representation multiple times under
       varying contexts by conditioning the formula Φ on a set of evidence literals E. While the
       d-DNNF language is theoretically closed under conditioning, meaning the logically restricted
       formula Φ[E] remains a valid d-DNNF, explicitly modifying the graph structure for every new
       query is computationally inefficient. Instead, practical implementations achieve conditioning
       implicitly by assigning a weight of zero to any literal leaf falsified by the evidence E. This
       approach effectively abstracts the computation into an algebraic framework, where the
       d-DNNF is evaluated over a specific semiring tailored to the target query (e.g., the Boolean
       semiring for satisfiability or the arithmetic semiring for model counting). As a result, it
       enables lightweight, repeated query execution without incurring the overhead of rewriting or
       duplicating the circuit.

       ▶ Example 3 (Ex. 2 cont.). In the d-DNNF depicted in Figure 1, the standard model count
       (represented by the blue integers) is computed by assigning a default weight of 1 to every
       literal leaf, corresponding to an empty evidence set (E = ∅). If the formula is instead
       conditioned on the evidence E = {a} (red integers), the weight of the leaf ¬a is dynamically
       set to 0. During the bottom-up evaluation pass, this zero weight naturally propagates,
       effectively pruning any branch containing ¬a and yielding the conditioned model count
       without altering the underlying DAG structure.

           Building upon this lightweight conditioning mechanism, decdnnf_rs leverages the struc-
       tural properties of the d-DNNF to execute a variety of complex reasoning tasks. Specifically,
       the framework focuses on five primary queries, all of which can be evaluated seamlessly
       under a given evidence set E. Generally, executing these queries requires the d-DNNF to
       be smooth, a structural property ensuring that all children of any disjunctive gate depend
       on the exact same set of variables. However, explicitly transforming a circuit to enforce
       strict smoothness can inadvertently increase its size and memory footprint. To mitigate this
       overhead, decdnnf_rs handles smoothness dynamically. Instead of permanently modifying
       the graph, the tool computes the set of variables involved in a node’s subgraph on demand.
       These sets are used to label disjunction node edges (represented in ⟨·⟩ in Figure 1) when

some variables appear in a child but not in the other one (see [26] for more information).
The queries are seamlessly adjusted to account for these missing variables only when required
by the request.

Satisfiability. Determining whether a formula is consistent under a given context (i.e., if
M(Φ[E]) ̸= ∅) is a fundamental check. While generally NP-complete for raw CNF, this
task is highly efficient on a d-DNNF. Because d-DNNF compilers eagerly prune universally
unsatisfiable branches during the offline phase, an unconditioned d-DNNF is trivially satis-
fiable as long as it is not the constant ⊥. However, when evaluated under an evidence set
E, satisfiability is determined through a single bottom-up traversal. Leaves falsified by E
evaluate to 0 (or ⊥), while consistent leaves evaluate to 1 (or ⊤). These values propagate
upward according to classical Boolean semantics: a decomposable ∧ gate evaluates to 1 if
and only if all its children evaluate to 1, whereas a deterministic ∨ gate evaluates to 1 if at
least one child evaluates to 1. The conditioned formula is satisfiable if and only if the root
node does not evaluate to 0, an operation that scales strictly linearly with the size of the
circuit.

▶ Example 4 (Ex. 2 cont.). The formula Φ is inherently satisfiable under an empty evidence
set. However, when conditioned on the evidence E = {a, b}, the restricted formula Φ[E]
becomes unsatisfiable. Evaluating this on the d-DNNF (Figure 1) sets the leaves ¬a and
¬b to 0, which propagates upward to evaluate the left deterministic ∨ gate to 0, ultimately
rendering the root node 0.

Model Enumeration. The enumeration problem, often referred to as AllSAT, consists of
generating the set of all satisfying assignments of a formula, M(Φ[E]), without redundancy.
Models are typically produced in one of two forms: complete or partial. A complete model
is a total assignment specifying a truth value for every variable in Var(Φ). Given the
combinatorial explosion of complete models in practical instances, partial models (or cubes)
are frequently preferred as a more compact representation. A partial assignment constitutes a
valid model if every total assignment extending it is also a satisfying assignment for the formula.
Mathematically, a partial model ω defined over a subset of variables X ⊆ Var(Φ) intrinsically
represents 2|Var(Φ)|−|X| distinct complete models. Enumerating these partial models is
particularly efficient on d-DNNF representations, as the task naturally maps to extracting a
set of disjoint paths from the root to the consistent leaves. To perform this extraction with
optimal efficiency, decdnnf_rs takes advantage of its lazy smoothing mechanism to leverage
the concept of model graph, as introduced in [26], ensuring a streamlined and redundancy-free
generation of disjoint partial models directly from the compiled circuit.

▶ Example 5 (Ex. 2 cont.). The formula Φ has six complete models: {a, ¬b, c, d}, {¬a, b, c, d},
{a, ¬b, c, ¬d}, {¬a, b, c, ¬d}, {a, ¬b, ¬c, d}, and {¬a, b, ¬c, d}. These can be represented
more compactly by the following four partial models: {a, ¬b, c}, {¬a, b, c}, {a, ¬b, ¬c, d},
and {¬a, b, ¬c, d}. Note that the first partial model {a, ¬b, c} covers two complete models
because variable d is left unassigned.

Model Counting. The Model Counting (#SAT) task involves determining the exact number
of satisfying assignments, denoted ∥Φ[E]∥, under a given context. While strictly #P-complete
for general CNF formulas, this counting reduces to a linear-time algebraic evaluation on
a d-DNNF. The computation is performed via a single bottom-up traversal. Exploiting
the decomposability property, the model count at any ∧ gate is simply the product of the

       counts of its children. Similarly, determinism allows an ∨ gate to sum the counts of its
       mutually exclusive children. Crucially, by dynamically tracking the free variables at each
       node, decdnnf_rs seamlessly injects the necessary powers of 2 to account for variables absent
       from a local subgraph. This ensures the exact count is computed on the fly without requiring
       prior structural smoothing of the circuit.

       ▶ Example 6 (Ex. 2 cont.). As illustrated in Figure 1, the unconditioned model count for the
       root is ∥Φ∥ = 6 (indicated by the blue integers). When conditioned on the evidence E = {a},
       the weight of the literal ¬a drops to 0. This zero propagates upward, effectively nullifying
       the ¬a ∧ b branch. The root’s total sum is consequently reduced, yielding a conditioned
       model count of ∥Φ[E]∥ = 3 (indicated by the red integers).

       Direct Access. The direct access query, denoted Access(Φ[E], k, τ ), retrieves the k-th
       satisfying assignment from the conditioned model space M(Φ[E]) according to a strict
       lexicographical order ≺τlex induced by a designated variable sequence τ . Because the d-DNNF
       representation supports both conditioning and model counting in polynomial time, this
       retrieval operation is also performed in polynomial time. Specifically, if k > ∥Φ[E]∥, the
       requested index exceeds the available models, and an error is returned. Otherwise, the
       extraction algorithm initializes an empty partial assignment σ = ∅ and a search interval I =
       [0, ∥Φ[E]∥]. It then iteratively selects the next variable x according to the ordering τ . At each
       step, it computes the model count of the negative branch, denoted c¬x = ∥Φ[E ∪ σ ∪ {¬x}]∥.
       If I.min + c¬x ≥ k, the target model resides in the negative branch; consequently, σ is
       updated to σ ∪ {¬x} and the search interval I narrows to [I.min, I.min + c¬x ]. Otherwise,
       the target model lies in the positive branch, so σ is updated to σ ∪ {x} and the interval
       I shifts to [I.min + c¬x + 1, I.max], where I.min and I.max denote the lower and upper
       endpoints of the current interval, respectively. This deterministic descent guarantees the
       exact retrieval of the k-th model.

       ▶ Example 7 (Ex. 1 cont.). With τ = (a, b, c, d), the first model is {¬a, b, ¬c, d} (word 0101),
       and the third is {¬a, b, c, d} (word 0111).

       Uniform Sampling. A uniform sampler G must select a model from M(Φ[E]) such that
       every valid assignment has an equal probability of 1/∥Φ[E]∥ of being chosen. One approach
       uses a randomly generated integer k ∈ {1, . . . , ∥Φ[E]∥} followed by a direct access query.
       As established, this ensures strict, seed-based reproducibility regardless of the underlying
       circuit structure [27]. Alternatively, structural top-down traversals [36] offer faster execution
       but yield results dependent on the specific DAG topology. More precisely, this method
       first annotates each gate N with its conditioned model count, denoted c(N ) (as depicted
       in Figure 1). Assuming, without loss of generality, that all internal gates are binary, the
       algorithm traverses the circuit starting from the root with a specific target index k ≤ c(N ).
       At each decomposable ∧ gate N = Nℓ ∧ Nr , the target k is split to recursively call Nℓ with
       1 + ⌊(k − 1)/c(Nr )⌋ and Nr with 1 + ((k − 1) mod c(Nr )). At each deterministic ∨ gate
       N = Nℓ ∨ Nr , the algorithm routes the search: if k ≤ c(Nℓ ), it recursively calls Nℓ with k;
       otherwise, it calls Nr with k − c(Nℓ ). To handle dynamic smoothness, an unsmoothed node
       N with a set of free variables V is treated conceptually as an ∧ gate Ng ∧ (⊤, V ). When
       retrieving the k-th assignment from the (⊤, V ) component, the algorithm uses a predefined
       variable ordering (x1 , . . . , x|V | ) and represents k − 1 as a bit-vector. The literal is set to
       ¬xi if the i-th bit is 0, and xi otherwise. Finally, when reaching a leaf, the corresponding
       literal is added to the computed model. Because different compilers, or different heuristic

Minimization via Semantic Hashing and Provenance Tracking. While d-DNNF circuits
facilitate efficient inference, they are susceptible to exponential blow-up in size, which
severely hampers scalability and storage efficiency [6]. This “tractability-vs-size” trade-off
presents a significant barrier to deploying KC in resource-constrained or large-scale scenarios.
Consequently, minimizing these compiled representations is a critical post-processing step.
State-of-the-art reduction frameworks, such as those inspired by FRAIGs (Functionally
Reduced And-Inverter Graphs), typically rely on SAT sweeping [3, 30, 22]. This process
involves incrementally solving a sequence of topologically ordered SAT problems to identify
and merge functionally equivalent nodes. However, a major bottleneck of this approach is the
sheer volume of solver calls required, which becomes computationally prohibitive for large
circuits. In [5], we proposed a novel minimization framework that avoids expensive SAT calls
by exploiting the inherent properties of the target language itself. Our key insight is that since
d-DNNF representations allow for polynomial-time model counting, we can leverage semantic
information (specifically model counts) to accelerate equivalence checking. We introduced a
specialized hashing mechanism that utilizes the model count and the variable set of each
node as a semantic signature. Unlike pure structural hashing, this hybrid approach integrates
both combinatorial and numerical properties to efficiently identify candidate sub-circuits
for merging. By computing these signatures, we can rapidly cluster structurally similar
components and drastically reduce the search space for equivalence testing. Furthermore, we
supplanted the traditional SAT-based verification step with a polynomial-time refinement
process. We achieve this by tagging the d-DNNF structure with metadata derived from the
original CNF formula. These CNF-based annotations allow us to trace the provenance of
sub-circuits and verify logical equivalence through a structured check, ensuring correctness
without reverting to NP-hard reasoning.

 4     The decdnnf_rs reasoner
Figure 2 illustrates the overarching architecture and typical workflow of the decdnnf_rs
framework, which is strictly divided into an offline compilation phase and an online querying
phase. During the offline phase, an initial propositional formula (typically in CNF) is
processed by an external, state-of-the-art knowledge compiler, such as d4, to generate an
equivalent d-DNNF circuit file. This computationally intensive compilation step is performed
only once. The online phase begins when this serialized d-DNNF file is passed to one of
the framework’s four distinct interfaces: a native Rust library for seamless embedding, a
comprehensive CLI (Command-Line Interface) for standalone execution, or Python and
C bindings for integration into data science pipelines and legacy codebases. As depicted
in the diagram, the user interacts exclusively with their chosen interface. The interface is
responsible for submitting the loaded circuit, along with any specific queries and evidence,

       down to the underlying decdnnf_rs core engine. The core engine then executes the advanced

       This decoupled architecture allows practitioners to repeatedly interact with the circuit to

           Regardless of the manipulation interface employed, the process always begins with loading
       a d-DNNF formula from a file. During this loading phase, decdnnf_rs performs validation
       checks to ensure the formula’s correctness. Errors are raised if unreachable nodes are detected
       or if a node violates the decomposability property. Furthermore, the library attempts to
       verify the determinism of disjunction nodes by searching for opposing literals within their
       children. However, as the absence of such opposing literals is not a definitive indicator of
       determinism, warnings are issued in these instances rather than errors. Since these checks
       can be computationally expensive, the possibility is let to the user to deactivate them.
           As previously discussed, decdnnf_rs natively processes the standard textual output
       generated by the d4 compiler. Because this format omits the total variable count, the engine
       infers it from the highest index present in the circuit. However, if this inferred maximum
       index differs from the actual variable count, the user can manually specify the true number
       of variables through the interface to ensure accurate query evaluation.
           When integrating the library or its bindings, a d-DNNF circuit is parsed only once,
       regardless of the number of subsequent queries. Conversely, to maintain a stateless and
       straightforward design, the CLI application does not support batching multiple queries within
       a single execution. As a result, the formula must be reloaded from disk for every individual
       query, which can introduce a substantial I/O bottleneck. To mitigate this overhead, the CLI
       includes a dedicated command that compiles the standard, text-based d-DNNF into a highly
       optimized binary format. Utilizing this binary representation drastically accelerates parsing,
       effectively minimizing the latency associated with repeated CLI invocations.
           The CLI application is designed for accessibility and ease of use. It features a comprehens-
       ive suite of commands that can be listed by invoking the root application with the --help
       flag. Detailed configuration options and usage instructions for any specific command are
       accessible by appending the --help flag to it.
           For repeated queries on a specific d-DNNF instance, directly integrating the decdnnf_rs
       library is highly recommended for optimal performance. First, it allows the formula to be
       loaded and parsed only once. This one-time initialization also covers essential preprocessing

steps, such as computations related to the dynamic tracking of the circuit’s smoothness.
Furthermore, the library minimizes I/O overhead by retaining query results in memory
rather than serializing them to the standard output. This optimization is particularly critical
when dealing with the massive result sets generated by sampling or enumeration tasks. For
instance, the framework’s parallel enumeration algorithm leverages direct access queries
to allow multiple threads to compute batches of models concurrently. While this parallel
speedup is largely bottlenecked by console I/O when using the CLI application, invoking the
algorithm directly via the library unlocks its full performance potential.
    The core Rust codebase, encompassing both the library and the CLI application, is open-
source and hosted on GitHub [23], with published packages available via crates.io [28].
Comparing to the versions of the tool used for [26] and [27], we added the ability to condition
the queries using assumption literals, we finalized the high-performance parallel enumeration
engine and we added the minimization algorithm from [5]. Additionally, dedicated C and
Python bindings are maintained in separate GitHub repositories [24, 25]. Note that the
C bindings require the GNU Multiple Precision Arithmetic Library (GMP) as a system
dependency. Comprehensive documentation and practical examples accompany the Rust
library; notably, the CLI application’s source code (located in the src/app directory) serves
as a primary, real-world reference implementation. Finally, it is important to emphasize that
parallel model enumeration is not supported within the Python bindings. Python’s Global
Interpreter Lock (GIL) fundamentally prevents true thread-based parallelism, which would
negate the concurrency performance gains achieved by the underlying decdnnf_rs engine.



 5     Conclusion and future work

In this paper, we introduced decdnnf_rs, a modular framework for performing advanced
reasoning tasks on d-DNNF circuits. By leveraging lightweight, implicit conditioning and
dynamic smoothness tracking, the tool provides efficient support for core queries such as
satisfiability, model counting, model enumeration, direct access, and uniform sampling.
Bridging the gap between theoretical knowledge compilation and practical software engin-
eering, decdnnf_rs serves as a robust foundation for both exact and stochastic automated
reasoning.
    For future work, we plan to extend the tool along several key dimensions. First, to
eliminate the I/O overhead of reloading the d-DNNF formula for consecutive queries, we
aim to design a formal query protocol that facilitates a persistent, network-based query
manager (e.g., a daemon or server mode). Architecturally, we will restructure the Rust
codebase by strictly decoupling the core library from the CLI application. This separation
will significantly reduce the dependency footprint for developers embedding decdnnf_rs into
their own projects.
    To broaden the tool’s applicability, we will expand the query repertoire to include standard
tasks such as Weighted Model Counting [35]. Furthermore, we plan to elevate the query
manager’s expressiveness by supporting high-level variables – such as categorical or numerical
types – allowing practitioners to formulate queries directly using domain-specific abstractions.
We also intend to develop a distributed variant of the engine for seamless integration with the
distributed knowledge compiler introduced in [39]. Finally, we aim to collaborate with the
broader knowledge compilation community to define a standardized binary exchange format.
This initiative will streamline integration with state-of-the-art compilers and drastically
reduce the parsing time currently incurred by verbose text formats.
